newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's DKB under fire as Nomura probe widens.
newsitem.headline: Japan's DKB under fire as Nomura probe widens.

text.p: Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), a leading Japanese commercial bank, was raided by prosecutors on Tuesday in an apparently widening investigation into links between racketeers and the world of finance.

DKB, the world's third biggest bank in terms of assets, said that it regretted the raid, but stayed silent over reports that it provided questionable loans to the racketeer at the centre of the Nomura Securities payoff scandal, Ryuichi Koike.

"We find it extremely regrettable that we have brought on ourselves a situation in which Tokyo prosecutors have searched (our offices). We will cooperate fully with investigations," a bank spokesman said.
He said he did not yet know the reason for the raid, and declined to comment on DKB's reported link with Koike.
"We do not comment on deals with our individual customers," the spokesman said.
Prosecutors would not immediately comment on the raid.
Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori Koike were arrested last week on suspicion of taking some 50 million yen ($438,000) in illegal payments from Nomura.
Two former Nomura executives and a third senior Nomura official have also been arrested in the case.
Japan's Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.
After the Nomura payoff scandal emerged in early March, media reports said DKB had loaned three billion yen ($26.3 million) in 1989 to the younger Koike's real estate firm.
The elder Koike reportedly used the money to buy 300,000 shares in each of the nation's top four brokerages, including Nomura, and put up the shares as collateral for DKB loans.
On Tuesday, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily said that DKB had provided questionable loans worth some 600 million yen ($5.26 million) in 1994 without collateral to Ryuichi Koike.
This was reported to be the latest chunk of a total of 30 billion yen ($263 million) in loans extended to Koike by DKB and a closely linked financial firm, Daiwa Shinyo.
DKB is still holding unrecoverable problem loans worth 7.5 billion yen ($65.7 million) and Daiwa Shinyo 1.2 billion yen ($10.5 million) from such loans, Japanese media reported.
The Yomiuri said prosecutors were particularly looking at whether the latest uncollaterised loans to Koike had violated the Commercial Code and involved breach of trust.
If DKB extended loans to the sokaiya without any collateral and was well aware that the loans would not be paid back, legal action could be brought, financial analysts have said.
But some analysts noted that many Japanese banks made insufficiently collateralised loans to shady characters during the late 1980s bubble economy era of inflated asset prices.
"If you go into the bubble era, all banks made loans to property dealers who may or may not have had shady pasts, or presents or futures," one analyst said.
Shares in Dai-Ichi Kangyo slid in Tokyo trading on Tuesday morning following reports of the raid.
"The share prices are being hammered, but...the actual impact on DKB is minimal in terms of the 7.5 billion yen loss, if that is correct," said Brian Waterhouse of HSCB James Capel.
He added: "The damage to their image, if there is going to be any at all, is going to be local rather than international."
The shares ended the morning session down 70 yen at 1,400 yen, ranking as the eighth most heavily traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

DKB is scheduled on Friday to announce its earnings for the business year which ended on March 31. The bank has forecast a parent current loss of 300 billion yen ($2.63 billion) for 1996/97 after disposing of about 550 billion yen ($4.82 billion) worth of problem loans in the year.
